problem: Navigation systems assume an obstacle-free path exists, and existing interactive navigation (NAMO) methods handle a single task at a time, often in pre-arranged scenes with full observability, ignoring how relocated objects persist and affect future tasks.
motivation: Real robots in homes or warehouses face sequential tasks in the same cluttered space, where each decision to move or bypass an obstacle changes future navigability. Success requires long-horizon, perception-aware reasoning, which chaining low-level LLM actions handles poorly; LLMs are better at abstract semantic reasoning.
key_idea: Recast a frozen LLM from action-sequence generator to a constraint reasoner over a structured scene graph (with blocking edges, betweenness centrality, and path costs) that chooses which obstacles to relocate, where to put them, and which room to explore, while a standard planner executes the primitives.
insight: Reasoning about a few high-level decisions with cost-benefit attributes, rather than low-level actions, enables zero-shot long-horizon planning. Baselines show the tradeoff: Always Interact and Clean+S/P pay heavy manipulation cost, Always Detour keeps bottlenecks, whereas CoReLIN interacts selectively (~28-38% interaction rate). The manipulation-cost ablation shows interaction drops about 4x from e=1 to e=20 while SR stays roughly stable. The run-through shows the LLM adapts to the remaining horizon: explore early, rearrange mid-episode, detour late.
method: Scene graph perception: an incrementally built grid graph of free space plus a directed graph of discovered objects and rooms, with blocking edges C_ij; unseen rooms are kept as frontier nodes.
Node attributes for the LLM: shortest-path cost to the object, blocking objects, normalized betweenness centrality of the occupied cell, and cost of an alternative path avoiding blockers.

LLM constraint planner: a frozen LLM (Gemini by default in the ablations, also GPT-5 and DeepSeek) reads the text serialization and selects among explore-room, navigate, or move-obstacle-to-placement, using cost = d(robot,obj)+2e+d(obj,zone) with e=5 s. The cost-benefit objective is only an abstraction, not explicitly optimized.
Task-directed exploration: the planner ranks unexplored rooms by semantic relevance to the task as a soft ordering and replans after each observation.
Low-level execution: candidates are filtered to reachable, feasible actions; Dijkstra navigation and reliable pick-place primitives execute; closed perceive-plan-act loop.

New metrics: Price of Clutter (PoC, ratio of cumulative shortest-path lengths in the cluttered vs. obstacle-free graph) and Long-term Efficiency Score (LES, weighted geometric mean of SR (0.5), normalized TS utility (0.25) and PoC utility (0.25)).
Benchmark: ProcTHOR-10k floorplans with 1-10 rooms, clutter sampled proportional to betweenness centrality, sequences of 10/15/20 object-to-receptacle tasks with no reset.

setting.backbone: Frozen LLM (Gemini / GPT-5 / DeepSeek) as high-level planner; Dijkstra planner and pick-place primitives for low level
setting.training_data: none (training-free, zero-shot); learned baselines were retrained on 10k generated episodes
setting.observation: Egocentric RGB-D with object detection / segmentation building a scene graph; the general floorplan (room count and adjacency) is known, room contents unknown. Real robot: front fisheye RGB-D + YOLO + SAM.
setting.action_space: High-level: explore room / move obstacle to placement / navigate to goal; low-level 0.25 m grid navigation and PickupObject/PutObject primitives (AI2-THOR)
setting.privileged: none for CoReLIN (unk); the CoReLIN (known) variant and all baselines get the full ground-truth map, objects and obstacles; floorplan room topology is known

numbers.extra: no prior knowledge of the world, must explore

numbers_note: Custom benchmark (100 test environments from ProcTHOR-10k, 1-10 rooms, grouped 1-3/4-6/7-10 with horizons g=10/15/20); only a subset of the 18 (horizon x room-bin x variant) cells is listed. The LLM used for the main table is not stated. The abstract's '16% over best baseline' is not directly traceable to a single table cell.
results: On the custom ProcTHOR lifelong benchmark, CoReLIN (known) obtains the best LES in medium and large floorplans across horizons (e.g. 81.62 vs 79.67 for Always Interact at g=10, 7-10 rooms; 86.56 vs 74.73 at g=20). The unknown-map variant is lower (LES 49.99 at g=20, 7-10 rooms) but far above learned baselines ADIN and InterNav, which reach ~3-17% SR. Heuristics such as Always Interact and Clean+S/P slightly win in small (1-3 room) environments.
limitations: Manipulation effort is a fixed constant and interaction is restricted to pick-and-place of small objects; the pick-place primitive is assumed reliable.

Main comparisons give baselines and the 'known' variant ground-truth maps, and the unknown variant degrades in large or dense scenes, mainly from missed object or receptacle discovery. LLM choice matters (GPT-5 degrades on larger floorplans).
Real-world validation is only qualitative on a single three-room setup with a precomputed grid; no quantitative hardware results.
